deforestation.explanation: India's Supreme Court ruled in 1996 (T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India) that "forest" should be read in its ordinary dictionary sense — any land with forest-like characteristics counts, whether or not it's officially notified as a forest in government records. A 2023 amendment to the Forest (Conservation) Act tried to narrow this to only officially declared or government-recorded forest land, which would exclude large areas of unclassed and community forest. In February 2025 the Supreme Court ordered the government to keep using the broader 1996 definition until every state finishes compiling a complete record of its forest land — a task most states still haven't finished decades on.
deforestation.source_note: Supreme Court of India, T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Union of India (1996); Supreme Court interim order, February 2025

deforestation.explanation: Under the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 (renamed the Van Adhiniyam in 2023), no state or authority may use forest land for a non-forest purpose — mining, roads, dams, industry — without prior approval from the central government. That approval process is called "diversion." It happens in two stages: an in-principle approval, followed by final clearance once the state confirms it has met the required conditions.

When forest land is diverted for another use, the law requires an equivalent (or larger, for non-forest land) area to be planted elsewhere to replace it, plus payment into a compensatory afforestation fund. CAG audits have repeatedly found this requirement poorly enforced — for example, one state audit found only about half of the required afforestation area was ever actually planted, despite fees being collected for it.
deforestation.source_note: Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980; CAG audit reports (see Karnataka case example on this dashboard)

deforestation.explanation: The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change told Parliament that 1,73,984.3 hectares of forest land were approved for diversion nationally between April 2014 and March 2024 — mining and hydropower were the largest categories. That's roughly the land area of a mid-sized Indian district, cleared for non-forest use over a decade, through the official, legal approval process — separate from any illegal or unapproved felling.
deforestation.source_note: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, reply to Lok Sabha, 2025

land-allocation.explanation: Government tenders are supposed to attract multiple competing bidders so prices and terms are tested by competition. A tender that receives only one bid isn't automatically improper — small or specialized contracts sometimes only attract one qualified bidder — but a pattern of large single-bid awards, especially to the same vendor repeatedly, is one of the standard red flags auditors and procurement watchdogs look for.
land-allocation.source_note: General public procurement audit practice; see CAG and CVC guidance on tender competitiveness

land-allocation.explanation: The Central Public Procurement Portal is the Indian government's official platform where central ministries, PSUs, and many state bodies are required to publish tenders and contract awards. It's a genuinely public record — anyone can look up who won a given government contract and for how much.
